request.system:
You explain a fitted credit-risk model to a credit risk manager who is not a data scientist. You receive the facts about one model and write a short explanation of what drives its predictions of default.

# The text

- Write 5 to 8 sentences in plain English, most important drivers first.
- Mention an interaction when it matters for the model's predictions.
- Say only what the facts support. Do not round a weak effect up to a strong one, and do not add knowledge about credit risk that the facts do not show.
- When the facts do not settle something, say so ("the data do not settle whether ...") or leave it out.

# The answer

Return one JSON object with one list, `sentences`, each with an `id` (1, 2, 3, ...) and its `text`.
messages:
These are the facts about the model.

Model: an explainable boosting machine (EBM), fitted to predict whether a credit applicant defaults (30,000 applicants). Effects are on the log-odds scale: positive values raise the risk of default. Every band is a 95% band from 100 refits of the model on resampled data.

Features, in the order of their share of the model's importance:
- `PAY_0`: repayment status in September 2005, the latest month (-1 paid in full, 1 to 9 months of payment delay; -2 and 0 are not in the data dictionary, commonly read as no consumption and revolving credit used).
  Share of importance 39.6% (95% band 36.6% to 42.6%); rank 1 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= -1: -0.2; 0: -0.5; 1: +0.6; >= 2: +2.3 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +2.57, 95% band [+2.46, +2.76]).
- `LIMIT_BAL`: amount of the given credit in NT dollars, individual and family (supplementary) credit.
  Share of importance 20.9% (95% band 18.3% to 23.2%); rank 2 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= 74999: +0.5; 75000-204999: -0.06; >= 205000: -0.4 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile -1.12, 95% band [-1.33, -0.95]).
- `BILL_AMT1`: amount of the bill statement in September 2005, the latest month, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 10.3% (95% band 5.8% to 11.9%); rank 3 to 5 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= 16982: -0.15; >= 16983: +0.1 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +0.67, 95% band [+0.41, +0.79]).
- `PAY_AMT1`: amount paid in September 2005, the latest month, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 9.3% (95% band 7.2% to 12.2%); rank 3 to 4 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= 1270: +0.18; >= 1271: -0.1 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile -0.58, 95% band [-0.75, -0.40]).
- `AGE`: age in years.
  Share of importance 4.7% (95% band 3.4% to 6.4%); rank 4 to 6 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): <= 42: 0; >= 43: +0.2 (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +0.34, 95% band [+0.18, +0.47]).
- `PAY_AMT2`: amount paid in August 2005, the month before, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 4.0% (95% band 1.7% to 6.0%); rank 5 to 7 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): no movement resolved at this sample size (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile -0.15, 95% band [-0.27, +0.02]).
- `BILL_AMT2`: amount of the bill statement in August 2005, the month before, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 1.7% (95% band 0.7% to 4.8%); rank 5 to 9 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): no movement resolved at this sample size (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile -0.04, 95% band [-0.26, +0.15]).
- `EDUCATION`: education (1 graduate school, 2 university, 3 high school, 4 others; 0, 5 and 6 are not in the data dictionary).
  Share of importance 1.0% (95% band 0.2% to 2.3%); rank 7 to 9 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): no movement resolved at this sample size (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +0.05, 95% band [-0.01, +0.14]).
- `PAY_AMT3`: amount paid in July 2005, two months before, in NT dollars.
  Share of importance 0.2% (95% band 0.2% to 2.1%); rank 7 to 9 among 9 features.
  Curve (logit contribution by value): no movement resolved at this sample size (net change from the 5th to the 95th percentile +0.01, 95% band [-0.07, +0.22]).

Interactions: the model has 5 pairs. The larger ones:
- `BILL_AMT1 & AGE`: share of importance 3.4% (95% band 2.0% to 4.3%).
  Effect of `BILL_AMT1` from 0 to 201,000: +0.92 (95% band +0.58 to +1.14) when `AGE` = 23, +0.30 (95% band +0.02 to +0.50) when `AGE` = 53.
  Effect of `AGE` from 23 to 53: +0.57 (95% band +0.32 to +0.73) when `BILL_AMT1` = 0, -0.05 (95% band -0.34 to +0.18) when `BILL_AMT1` = 201,000.
- `AGE & BILL_AMT2`: share of importance 1.8% (95% band 0.9% to 2.5%).
  Effect of `AGE` from 23 to 53: +0.29 (95% band +0.05 to +0.50) when `BILL_AMT2` = 0, +0.14 (95% band -0.03 to +0.37) when `BILL_AMT2` = 195,000.
  Effect of `BILL_AMT2` from 0 to 195,000: +0.06 (95% band -0.27 to +0.25) when `AGE` = 23, -0.10 (95% band -0.36 to +0.09) when `AGE` = 53.
- `PAY_0 & EDUCATION`: share of importance 1.7% (95% band 0.0% to 2.1%).
  Effect of `PAY_0` from -2 to 2: +2.42 (95% band +2.33 to +2.65) when `EDUCATION` = 1, +2.85 (95% band +2.49 to +3.04) when `EDUCATION` = 3.
  Effect of `EDUCATION` from 1 to 3: -0.09 (95% band -0.21 to +0.08) when `PAY_0` = -2, +0.34 (95% band +0.01 to +0.43) when `PAY_0` = 2.
- `PAY_AMT2 & AGE`: share of importance 0.8% (95% band 0.0% to 1.7%).
  Effect of `PAY_AMT2` from 0 to 19,000: -0.08 (95% band -0.23 to +0.08) when `AGE` = 23, -0.22 (95% band -0.43 to +0.02) when `AGE` = 53.
  Effect of `AGE` from 23 to 53: +0.36 (95% band +0.17 to +0.49) when `PAY_AMT2` = 0, +0.23 (95% band -0.02 to +0.49) when `PAY_AMT2` = 19,000.
- `PAY_AMT1 & AGE`: share of importance 0.8% (95% band 0.0% to 1.6%).
  Effect of `PAY_AMT1` from 0 to 18,400: -0.65 (95% band -0.88 to -0.40) when `AGE` = 23, -0.56 (95% band -0.82 to -0.41) when `AGE` = 53.
  Effect of `AGE` from 23 to 53: +0.35 (95% band +0.18 to +0.49) when `PAY_AMT1` = 0, +0.44 (95% band +0.12 to +0.64) when `PAY_AMT1` = 18,400.

Write the explanation.

content.text: {"sentences":[{"id":1,"text":"The model's predictions of default are driven mainly by repayment status in the latest month, September 2005, which accounts for about 40% of its importance: applicants who were already one or more months behind on payments carry a substantially higher predicted risk, with the effect rising sharply once delays reach two months or more."},{"id":2,"text":"The amount of credit granted is the second most important driver, at about 21% of importance: smaller credit limits (up to roughly 75,000 NT dollars) push predicted risk up, while larger limits (205,000 NT dollars and above) push it down, with a net swing from the 5th to the 95th percentile of about -1.1 on the log-odds scale."},{"id":3,"text":"The September bill amount and September payment amount each matter to a lesser degree, at roughly 10% and 9% of importance; larger bills nudge risk up slightly, while larger payments nudge it down, though both effects are small compared with repayment status and credit limit."},{"id":4,"text":"Age plays a minor, more modest role, at about 5% of importance, with applicants aged 43 and over carrying slightly higher predicted risk than younger ones."},{"id":5,"text":"Age interacts with the September bill amount: the bill amount raises predicted risk more for younger applicants (around age 23) than for older ones (around age 53), and the age effect itself is strongest when the bill amount is zero."},{"id":6,"text":"The repayment-status effect also varies somewhat with education, with the risk increase from delayed payments appearing larger for applicants with high school education than for graduate-school applicants, though this interaction is weaker and its uncertainty is wide."},{"id":7,"text":"The August bill and payment amounts, the earlier-month payment amount, and education on its own add little to the predictions, and the data do not clearly establish their direction of effect."}]}
